name_en: Xin Gong Yi Bai Cha (New-Process White Tea)
cultivar: Fuding Dabai, Fuding Dahao and Cai Cha
processing: A shortened wither followed by a brief, light rolling and a slightly warmer drying, so the leaf curls, darkens and oxidises a little more than classic white tea; made mostly from Mudan- and Shou Mei-grade leaf.
harvest_season: Spring and autumn, from the leafier pickings; sold without much emphasis on date.
appearance_dry: Semi-curled, slightly twisted leaves in dark green and brown, more compact than Shou Mei.
appearance_liquor: Orange-gold, deeper than classic white tea.
appearance_wet: Curled olive-brown leaves with reddish edges, opening less fully than unrolled white tea.
taste_profile: Fuller and fruitier than classic white tea, with stewed apple, honey and a light toasted note, a touch of oolong-like roundness and a smooth, sweet finish.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or pot at 90–95 °C. Behaves like a light oolong: the rolled leaf opens over a few steeps and holds its flavour well.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year tea without much fuss about season, loose or pressed, and in Hong Kong and South-East Asia (its original markets) often aged for years in shops and homes. It is a small niche beside classic Fujian white and is usually cheap; some of it is sold simply as 'white tea' without the process being named.
description:
Xin Gong Yi Bai Cha, 'new-process white tea', is Fuding's answer to a 1960s export request: Hong Kong buyers wanted a white tea with more colour and body than the pale traditional kind, and in 1968 the Baiqin tea factory in Fuding worked out a way to give it to them. The trick was to add a brief, light rolling after a shortened wither and dry it a little warmer, which curls the leaf, darkens it and pushes oxidation up a notch.

That one extra step makes it a different tea. Classic white tea is never rolled, so its cell structure stays intact and the flavour is slow and subtle; a lightly rolled leaf releases more, oxidises more at the edges and brews up orange rather than pale gold. It is made mostly from the leafier Mudan and Shou Mei pickings rather than from buds.

In the cup it is fuller and fruitier than any classic white: stewed apple and honey, a light toasted note, a roundness that recalls a gentle oolong, and a smooth sweet finish with no bitterness. It takes near-boiling water, 90–95 °C, and six steeps from a gaiwan, and it is one of the few white teas that makes sense in a teapot for a Western-style brew. Aged, it leans further into dried fruit.

It is a niche tea now, overshadowed by the boom in classic Fujian whites, and it is cheap. Sellers in Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore often have older stock, since it was made for those markets and ages comfortably; in the West it turns up occasionally, sometimes just labelled 'white tea' with the curled leaf as the only clue. If you see rolled, dark, curled 'white tea' from Fuding at a low price, this is probably what it is, and it is worth a try.

It is a useful bridge tea: for an oolong drinker curious about whites, or a white-tea drinker wondering what a little rolling does.
sources_note: The 1968 Baiqin factory origin is the standard Chinese account; not independently verified.
